newsitem.title: LIBERIA: Liberians cautious on new election timetable.
newsitem.headline: Liberians cautious on new election timetable.

text.p: Liberians weary of seven years of civil war welcomed the latest timetable for presidential elections with a mixture of hope and apprehension on Thursday.
West African leaders meeting in the Nigerian capital Abuja on Wednesday agreed to postpone the election to July 19 from May 30, saying the previous date was no longer possible.

Most residents of the capital Monrovia still fear violence and harassment and are uncertain whether to trust assurances from West African ECOMOG peacekeepers that they have disarmed many fighters and the country is secure enough for elections.

"We still don't feel a sense of a level playing field for these elections. The warlords still have their influence in the hinterland," said businessman Mohammed Sesay, who was among ethnic Mandingos attacked last weekend in warlord Charles Taylor's former stronghold of Gbarnga.
Former rebel fighters loyal to Taylor disrupted a prayer service organised by the Bong County Mandingos Development Association in Gbarnga, wounding a dozen people.
On Tuesday, thugs in Gbarnga prevented members of the party formed by Taylor's rival Alhaji Kromah from hoisting a party flag and entering an office building.

"ECOMOG is telling us security is good, yet at the same time ECOMOG continues to recover heavy weapons in the counties where we will be campaigning," said Madison Wion, formerly a leading member of Krahn warlord Roosevelt Johnson's ULIMO-J faction.

Taylor, who launched the civil war in December 1989, has said he will run in the elections. Other candidates include Kromah and Ellen Johnson-Sirleaf, the respected Africa director of the United Nations Development Programme.

Freed American slaves founded Liberia in 1847. The war has killed more than 150,000 people and displaced half the pre-war population of 2.5 million. Hundreds of thousands of Liberians are refugees in neighbouring Ivory Coast, Guinea and Sierra Leone. Others are in Ghana and Nigeria.
The latest delay in the much-postponed elections could cause logistical problems. July to September is the wettest period of Liberia's rainy season, when most of the interior is inaccessible by road.
"It is not the best of times in Liberia. The only good time in Liberia would be the second week of October," said U.N. special representative to Liberia Tuliameni Kalomoh.
The electoral commission had said the poll would cost $10 million, but the Abuja meeting cut the budget to $4.1 million.
The 16 members of the Economic Community of West African States, according to a communique published in Monrovia on Thursday, pledged $100,000 each towards the election budget.
Liberia's interim government will provide $500,000 as its contribution. Finance Minister Lansanah Kromah told the interim parliament on Wednesday his ministry had made an initial payment of $125,000.
If the new president is elected in the first round, the swearing-in would take place on August 2. If a runoff is needed, it would be on August 2 and the inauguration would be on August 16.

"I hope the date is good enough for everyone so that this nightmare can end and our people restart their normal activities," Liberian footballer George Weah told Reuters from Italy, where he plays for AC Milan.
